title: Lexicographic Rank of a String
directAnswer: Find the 1-based rank of a string among all its permutations in dictionary order. For each position, count how many characters to its right are smaller — each such smaller character could lead a block of (remaining-length)! permutations that all sort before the given string. Sum those blocks and add 1. With duplicate characters you must divide each block by the factorials of the repeated counts. Distinct case is O(n²) or O(n·26); answer rank = 1 + Σ (smaller-to-right) × (remaining)!.

remember.pattern: Factorial number system: count permutations that sort before each prefix
remember.formula:
DISTINCT:   rank = 1 + Σ_i  smallerRight(i) * (n-1-i)!
WITH DUPLICATES: rank = 1 + Σ_i  smallerRight(i) * (n-1-i)! / Π_c (freq[c]!)
  where freq is the frequency of the suffix s[i..n-1], updated as you advance
rules: Rank is **1-based** — the smallest permutation has rank 1, so the final answer adds 1.
`smallerRight(i)` counts characters strictly less than `s[i]` among positions `i+1..n-1`, **not** the whole string.
Each smaller character fixes position `i` and frees `(n-1-i)!` arrangements of the rest — that's why the factorial appears.
**Duplicates**: divide each block by `Π freq[c]!` over the current suffix multiset, or you over-count identical arrangements.
Factorials explode — `21!` overflows 64-bit. Use big integers, or compute the rank modulo a prime with modular inverses.
whenToUse: Rank / un-rank a permutation in lexicographic order
Map a permutation to/from an index (factorial number system)
Find the k-th permutation, or how many permutations precede a given one
Any 'position in dictionary of all rearrangements' question
antiSignals: You only need the *next* permutation → next_permutation in-place swap, not full ranking
Alphabet/length tiny and you just need any one answer → brute force all permutations
Strings are not permutations of each other → ranking among permutations is undefined
You need rank among arbitrary strings of a length, not permutations → positional base-Σ counting instead
remember.takeaway: Lexicographic rank is the factorial number system in disguise: digit i is 'how many unused smaller characters remain', weighted by the factorial of the remaining length. Duplicates just divide out the indistinguishable rearrangements.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can convert 'position in sorted order' into a per-position combinatorial count, and whether you correctly divide by repeated-character factorials instead of assuming all characters are distinct.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Counting smaller characters over the whole string instead of only to the right, forgetting the +1 for 1-based rank, or ignoring duplicates and over-counting.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the formula from the factorial number system, handle duplicates with the Π freq! division, and flag the overflow with a modular-inverse or big-integer plan.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, return its **1-based rank** among all distinct permutations of its characters, listed in lexicographic (dictionary) order.

The smallest permutation has rank 1. If `s` contains repeated characters, count each distinct arrangement once.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 20 if using 64-bit factorials; larger n needs big integers or modular arithmetic
understanding: Lay out every distinct rearrangement of the characters in dictionary order and ask which line the given string falls on. Instead of generating that list, count — for each position — how many permutations begin with a smaller-but-valid character, because all of those come earlier. Duplicates mean some arrangements coincide, so the per-block factorial must be deflated by the repeated counts.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the rank 0-based or 1-based?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 1-based by convention — the smallest permutation is rank 1. Confirm, because it changes only the final +1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the string have duplicate characters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, and it matters: identical arrangements must be counted once, which means dividing each factorial block by the factorials of the repeated counts.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can n be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If n ≤ 20, factorials fit in 64-bit. Beyond that, use big integers or compute the rank modulo a large prime with modular inverses.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are we ranking among permutations or among all strings of that length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Among permutations of the given multiset of characters. Ranking among all length-n strings is a different, base-Σ counting problem.

examples.explanation: Permutations sorted: abc, acb, bac, bca, cab, cba. "acb" is the 2nd → rank 2. At position 0, 'a' has nothing smaller to its right; at position 1, 'c' has 'b' smaller to its right → 1 × 1! = 1; plus 1 = 2.
All characters distinct; apply rank = 1 + Σ smallerRight(i) × (5−i)!.
Distinct permutations sorted: aab, aba, baa. "aba" is 2nd. Duplicate 'a' forces dividing each block by 2! where the suffix still holds two a's.

diagrams.title: Why each smaller character contributes a factorial block
diagrams.caption: Fixing a smaller character at position i frees (n-1-i)! arrangements of the rest — all of which sort before s.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Generate and Sort Permutations
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to nail the definition of rank, then point out the n! blow-up that forces the combinatorial formula.
hints: Generate every distinct permutation, sort them lexicographically, and the index of s (plus 1) is the rank.
Deduplicate with a set so repeated characters don't inflate the count.
There are up to n! permutations — this is only viable for very small n, but it nails down exactly what 'rank' means.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Generating permutations is O(n!) of them, each of length n; sorting that many length-n strings is O(n! · n log(n!)). Storing them is O(n! · n). Factorial growth caps this at roughly n ≤ 10.
approaches.explanation:
The definition-driven baseline literally builds the dictionary.

**The literal method.** Produce all permutations of the characters, drop duplicates into a sorted structure, and find where `s` lands. Its 1-based position is the rank.

**Why dedup matters.** With repeated characters, naive permutation generation yields the same string multiple times. A set (or sorted unique list) collapses those so each distinct arrangement counts once — matching the problem's definition.

**Why it can't scale.** The number of permutations is `n!` (or `n!/Πfreq!` distinct ones). For `n = 12` that's already ~479 million. Generating and sorting them is hopeless past tiny `n`. The value of this approach is purely as a correctness oracle and as a way to *see* that rank = (position in the sorted list) + 1 — the very quantity the combinatorial formula computes directly.
approaches.insight: Brute force shows that rank equals the count of distinct permutations strictly smaller than s, plus one. The optimal approach computes that count without materializing the list — by counting, position by position, how many smaller permutations exist.

dryRun.intro: List all distinct permutations in order and find the position of s.

java.line: private final TreeSet<String> perms = new TreeSet<>();
java.explanation: TreeSet keeps permutations sorted and deduplicated in one structure.
Position in sorted order (1-based) is the rank.

python.line: perms = sorted(set("".join(p) for p in permutations(s)))
python.explanation: set() dedups identical arrangements from repeated characters.

diagrams.caption: Rank is the 1-based index of s in this list.

pitfalls: Not deduplicating — repeated characters inflate the rank.
Returning a 0-based index — off by one from the expected 1-based rank.
Trying it for n beyond ~10 — n! permutations exhaust time and memory.

approaches.name: Factorial Counting with Duplicate Handling (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Derive it from the factorial number system and handle duplicates with the Π freq! division.
hints: Walk left to right. At position i, every permutation that puts a character smaller than s[i] here (and is otherwise any arrangement of the rest) sorts before s. How many such arrangements are there?
If the remaining characters are all distinct, fixing one smaller character leaves (n-1-i)! arrangements. Sum (count of smaller chars to the right) × (n-1-i)! over all i, then add 1.
With duplicates, (n-1-i)! over-counts because swapping identical characters yields the same string. Divide by the product of factorials of the remaining character frequencies.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of the n positions you count smaller characters in the suffix (O(Σ) with a frequency table, or O(n) by scanning), and compute a factorial-ratio block. That's O(n·Σ) or O(n²). The frequency table is O(Σ) space; factorials are precomputed in O(n).
approaches.explanation:
The optimal solution counts the permutations smaller than `s` directly, treating the answer as a number written in the factorial base.

**The per-position question.** Scan `s` left to right. Standing at position `i`, ask: how many distinct permutations agree with `s` on positions `0..i−1` but place a *smaller* character at position `i`? Every such permutation is lexicographically less than `s`, and every permutation less than `s` is captured at exactly one such position (the first place it diverges). So summing these counts over all `i` gives the number of permutations before `s`; add 1 for the 1-based rank.

**Counting one position (distinct case).** Let `smaller = ` the number of characters strictly less than `s[i]` among the *remaining* characters (positions `i..n−1`). Choosing any one of those smaller characters to sit at position `i` leaves `n−1−i` characters to arrange freely, which is `(n−1−i)!` orderings. So position `i` contributes `smaller × (n−1−i)!`.

**The duplicate correction.** When the remaining characters contain repeats, `(n−1−i)!` counts arrangements that are actually identical (swapping two equal characters changes nothing). The number of *distinct* arrangements of a multiset with frequencies `freq[c]` is `(n−1−i)! / Π_c freq[c]!`. So each block becomes `smaller × (n−1−i)! / Π_c freq[c]!`, where `freq` is the frequency table of the suffix `s[i..n−1]`. After processing position `i`, decrement `freq[s[i]]` so the table always reflects 'characters still available'.

**Why this is the factorial number system.** The sequence of `smaller` counts is exactly the factorial-base digits of `rank − 1`: digit `i` lies in `[0, n−1−i]` and carries weight `(n−1−i)!`. Ranking a permutation is reading off those digits; un-ranking (finding the k-th permutation) is the inverse.

**Overflow reality.** Factorials grow past 64-bit at `21!`. For larger inputs, either use big integers, or — if only `rank mod M` is needed — precompute factorials and modular inverses modulo a prime so the division by `Π freq!` becomes multiplication by modular inverses.
approaches.insight: Rank is a counting problem, not a sorting problem. Each position contributes an independent block of 'permutations that diverge here and go smaller', and the factorial weight is just the number of ways to fill the tail. Duplicates only change the weight by deflating it with Π freq! — the structure is identical.

dryRun.intro: Suffix frequency table drives the duplicate division. n = 3.

code.python:
from math import factorial


def rank(s: str) -> int:
    n = len(s)
    freq = [0] * 256
    for ch in s:
        freq[ord(ch)] += 1

    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        c = ord(s[i])
        smaller = sum(freq[ch] for ch in range(c))

        denom = 1
        for f in freq:
            denom *= factorial(f)
        # distinct arrangements of the suffix with one smaller char fixed in front,
        # summed over all smaller chars: smaller * (n-1-i)! / Π freq!
        block = smaller * factorial(n - 1 - i) // denom
        total += block

        freq[c] -= 1
    return total + 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(rank("aba"))
    print(rank("string"))

java.line: for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) fact[i] = fact[i - 1].multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(i));
java.explanation: Precompute factorials as BigInteger so 21! and beyond don't overflow.

java.line: for (int ch = 0; ch < c; ch++) smaller += freq[ch];
java.explanation: Count characters strictly smaller than s[i] still available in the suffix.
block = smaller × (n−1−i)! / Π freq! — the duplicate-aware count of permutations diverging here.
Consume s[i]; the suffix multiset shrinks before the next position.
+1 converts the count-of-smaller into a 1-based rank.

python.line: smaller = sum(freq[ch] for ch in range(c))
python.explanation: Characters smaller than s[i] remaining in the suffix (handles duplicates via counts).
Π freq! over the current suffix multiset (includes s[i] for now).
Distinct permutations that place a smaller char here; integer division is exact.
Remove s[i] from the available multiset before advancing.

diagrams.title: Per-position smaller-to-right counts
diagrams.caption: Each position's count times its factorial weight builds the rank.

pitfalls: Counting smaller characters over the whole string instead of only the suffix.
Ignoring duplicates — without the Π freq! division you over-count and inflate the rank.
Using 64-bit factorials beyond 20! — silent overflow to wrong (often negative) values.
Forgetting the +1, returning a 0-based count instead of a rank.

edgeCases.behavior: Only one distinct permutation → rank 1; duplicate division cancels everything.

commonMistakes: Counting smaller characters across the whole string rather than only positions to the right.
Treating duplicates as distinct and over-counting permutations.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Smaller count over the whole string
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Only characters still available (to the right) can validly sit at position i. Counting smaller characters that already appeared in the prefix double-counts and corrupts the rank.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: smaller = sum(1 for ch in s if ch < s[i])   # whole string — wrong
commonMistakesDetailed.good: smaller = sum(freq[ch] for ch in range(ord(s[i])))  # only remaining suffix

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ignoring duplicate characters
commonMistakesDetailed.why: (n-1-i)! counts arrangements that are identical when characters repeat. Without dividing by Π freq! the block over-counts and the rank comes out too large.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: block = smaller * factorial(n - 1 - i)            # over-counts duplicates
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
denom = 1
for f in freq:
    denom *= factorial(f)
block = smaller * factorial(n - 1 - i) // denom

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 64-bit factorial overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: 21! exceeds the 64-bit range, so for longer strings the factorial silently wraps and every block is wrong. Use big integers or modular arithmetic.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: long f = 1; for (int k = 2; k <= n; k++) f *= k; // overflows at 21!
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
BigInteger f = BigInteger.ONE;
for (int k = 2; k <= n; k++) f = f.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(k));

followupVariations.title: k-th Permutation Sequence (un-rank)
followupVariations.hint: Invert the formula: peel off factorial-base digits of k−1 to pick each character in turn.

followupVariations.title: Next Permutation
followupVariations.hint: If you only need the immediately following permutation, do the in-place pivot-swap-reverse in O(n).

followupVariations.title: Rank of a String mod p (large n)
followupVariations.hint: Precompute factorials and modular inverses; replace division by Π freq! with multiplication by inverses.

followupVariations.title: Rank Among All Strings of Length n
followupVariations.hint: Not a permutation problem — use positional base-Σ counting instead of factorials.

patternNote: Factorial Number System / combinatorial ranking. Recognise it whenever a problem asks for the position of a permutation in sorted order, the k-th permutation, or how many arrangements precede one — all are factorial-base digit reads, with duplicates handled by dividing out Π freq!.
